lessons.title: Macbeth: themes
lessons.summary: Explore the big ideas in Macbeth: ambition, kingship and tyranny, guilt, the supernatural and fate, appearance versus reality, and gender, and learn to link each theme to quotations and context.
objectives: I can explain how Shakespeare presents ambition as a destructive force and support this with quotations from across the play.
I can compare good kingship (Duncan, Malcolm) with tyranny (Macbeth) and link this to the Jacobean context.
I can track the theme of guilt through both Macbeth and Lady Macbeth.
I can explain how the supernatural, appearance versus reality and ideas about gender drive the action.
I can write a theme-based analytical paragraph that links point, evidence, method and context.

activities.title: Ambition: the engine of the tragedy
activities.content:
## Ambition

Ambition is the flaw that drives the whole play. Shakespeare does not present ambition as evil in itself: Macbeth is already a successful, admired soldier. The problem is **unchecked** ambition, desire that pushes past conscience, loyalty and law.

**How the theme develops**

- **The spark (1.3).** The witches' prophecy does not create Macbeth's ambition; it wakes something already there. His *"horrible imaginings"* show that he thinks of murder within moments.
- **The struggle (1.7).** In his soliloquy he admits he has no motive except *"Vaulting ambition, which o'erleaps itself / And falls on the other"*. The image of a rider jumping too high and crashing predicts his own fall.
- **The cost (Act 3).** Being king is not enough. He fears Banquo's sons will inherit, so ambition turns into paranoia and more murder.
- **The emptiness (Act 5).** Having gained everything, he finds life *"signifying nothing"*. Ambition has delivered a crown but destroyed everything that gave life meaning.

**Lady Macbeth's ambition** is just as fierce, but it is ambition *for* her husband and for the status she will share. Her collapse shows the same pattern: the prize is won, and the winners are ruined.

**Exam tip:** always show ambition as a *process* across the play, not a single moment.

activities.title: Worked analysis: ambition and imagery
activities.content:
**Question:** How does Shakespeare use imagery to present ambition as dangerous?

**Model paragraph**

Shakespeare presents ambition as a force that destroys its owner through the metaphor of *"Vaulting ambition, which o'erleaps itself"* (1.7). The verb *"vaulting"* suggests energy and athletic confidence, but *"o'erleaps"* turns the leap into a fall: the rider jumps so hard that he lands on the far side of the horse. Macbeth is, in effect, predicting his own downfall before he has acted, which makes his decision to continue even more tragic. Earlier, he asks *"Stars, hide your fires; / Let not light see my black and deep desires"* (1.4). The contrast of light and darkness shows he already knows his ambition belongs to the dark, so he wants to hide it even from heaven. A Jacobean audience would have seen this ambition as sinful pride, the same sin that made Lucifer fall, so the imagery of falling connects Macbeth's personal flaw to a religious warning.

**Why it scores well:** clear point, embedded quotations, close analysis of single words, and a context link that grows out of the language rather than being bolted on.

question.text: In Act 1 Scene 7, what does Macbeth admit is his only reason for killing Duncan?
question.hint: He lists many reasons *against* the murder first, then names one thing that pushes him towards it.
question.explanation: Macbeth says he has no spur except 'vaulting ambition'. He recognises that Duncan is a good king and his guest, so ambition is the only motive.

options.text: Revenge for an insult from Duncan
options.feedback: Duncan has just rewarded Macbeth, not insulted him.

options.text: A direct order from the witches
options.feedback: The witches only predict; they never tell him to kill.

options.text: Fear that Duncan plans to execute him

activities.title: Kingship and tyranny
activities.content:
## Kingship and tyranny

Shakespeare sets up a clear contrast between a **rightful king** and a **tyrant**.

**Duncan: the good king.** He is generous (rewarding Macbeth with a new title), humble and trusting. Even Macbeth admits Duncan *"Hath borne his faculties so meek, hath been / So clear in his great office"* (1.7). His murder is presented as an attack on the natural order: the night is stormy, horses eat each other, and daylight is swallowed by darkness (2.4).

**Macbeth: the tyrant.** He rules through fear and spies (*"There's not a one of them but in his house / I keep a servant fee'd"*, 3.4). Scotland becomes a place where, as Macduff says, *"each new morn / New widows howl"* (4.3). A tyrant, in Jacobean thinking, is a king who serves himself rather than his people.

**Malcolm: the restored king.** In Act 4 Scene 3 he tests Macduff by pretending to be worse than Macbeth, then lists the *"king-becoming graces"*: justice, mercy, temperance, courage. His victory promises order returned.

**Context link:** James I, the new king when the play was written, had himself written about the difference between a true king and a tyrant, and claimed descent from Banquo. The play flatters James and warns against those who would remove a rightful king, only a year after the Gunpowder Plot.

activities.title: Connecting kingship to disorder
activities.content:
A high-level essay links **kingship** to **natural order**. Use this three-step chain.

| Step | Idea | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Rightful king = natural order | Duncan compares Macbeth to a plant he will *"labour / To make thee full of growing"* (1.4) | Growth and nurture imagery |
| 2. Regicide = order broken | *"'Tis unnatural, / Even like the deed that's done"* (2.4): the Old Man on darkness at noon and Duncan's horses turning wild | Unnatural events mirror an unnatural act |
| 3. Tyranny = a sick country | Macbeth asks the doctor to *"find her disease / And purge it to a sound and pristine health"* (5.3), while Scotland itself is described as bleeding | Illness imagery |

**Sentence starter:** "Shakespeare links kingship to the health of the land itself, so that Macbeth's tyranny is felt as a kind of sickness, while Malcolm's return is presented as a cure."

This approach turns a list of quotations into an **argument about how the theme works**, which is what examiners reward.

question.text: Explain **two** ways Shakespeare shows that Macbeth is a tyrant rather than a rightful king, and link one of them to the play's Jacobean context.
question.hint: Think about how he rules (fear, spies, murder of the innocent) and what the audience of 1606 believed about rightful kings.
question.explanation: Macbeth rules through fear and spies, murders Banquo and the innocent Macduff family, and Scotland is described as suffering and sick. James I had written about the difference between a king who serves his people and a tyrant who serves himself, and the Divine Right of Kings meant removing a rightful king was seen as a crime against God.

markScheme.criterion: AO1: Gives one way Macbeth acts as a tyrant (spies, fear, murdering Banquo or the Macduff family, Scotland suffering)
AO1: Gives a second, different way (contrast with Duncan's generosity or Malcolm's graces, illness imagery, ruling for himself)
AO3: Links to Jacobean context (James I, Divine Right, Gunpowder Plot, ideas about tyrants)

activities.title: Guilt and conscience
activities.content:
## Guilt

Guilt is the theme that shows Shakespeare's interest in the **mind** rather than just the crime.

**Macbeth's guilt is immediate and loud.** Straight after the murder he hears a voice cry *"Macbeth does murder sleep"* (2.2) and asks whether the whole ocean can wash the blood from his hand. He sees a floating dagger before the murder and Banquo's ghost after it (3.4). His guilt does not stop him killing; instead he tries to bury it under more violence, deciding *"I am in blood / Stepp'd in so far"* that going back would be as hard as going on.

**Lady Macbeth's guilt is delayed and silent.** In Act 2 she claims *"A little water clears us of this deed"*. But in the sleepwalking scene (5.1) she rubs her hands endlessly, and the doctor hears her confess in fragments. Her mind has done what her will refused to do. She dies off stage, and Malcolm reports that she took her own life.

**Key motifs**
- **Blood**: from honourable battle blood to the stain that cannot be washed.
- **Sleep**: the innocent sleep; the guilty cannot rest.
- **Hands**: the instrument of the deed becomes the symbol of the guilt.

**Big idea:** guilt in the play is not a punishment from outside. It grows from within, which is why Lady Macbeth, who thought she could control it, is destroyed by it.

question.text: Match each quotation to the theme it most clearly illustrates.
question.hint: Think about what each image is really about: a stain, a disguise, a prediction, or a challenge to be a man.
question.explanation: 'Out, damned spot!' is Lady Macbeth's guilt made visible. 'Look like the innocent flower' is about hiding true intentions (appearance versus reality). 'All hail, Macbeth, that shalt be king hereafter' is the witches' prophecy. 'When you durst do it, then you were a man' is Lady Macbeth attacking Macbeth's masculinity.

pairs.left: "Look like the innocent flower, / But be the serpent under 't"
"All hail, Macbeth, that shalt be king hereafter"
"When you durst do it, then you were a man"

activities.title: The supernatural, fate and free will
activities.content:
## The supernatural and fate

The play opens with the witches, and the supernatural never leaves it: prophecies, a floating dagger, a ghost, apparitions and Hecate.

**Do the witches control Macbeth?** This is the key debate.

- **Fate argument:** the witches predict accurately, and everything they say comes true. Macbeth calls them *"imperfect speakers"* but still acts on their words.
- **Free will argument:** they never tell Macbeth what to do. Banquo hears the same prophecy and does nothing wrong. Macbeth chooses to murder, chooses to kill Banquo, and chooses to trust the second prophecies. Banquo warns that *"instruments of darkness tell us truths, / Win us with honest trifles, to betray's / In deepest consequence"* (1.3).

The strongest essays argue that the witches **tempt** rather than **compel**: they show Macbeth a possible future, and his own ambition does the rest. The **equivocation** of the later prophecies (no man *"of woman born"*, Birnam Wood moving) shows how the supernatural tells the truth in a way designed to mislead.

**Context:** James I believed in witches, wrote *Daemonologie* (1597) and supervised witch trials. A Jacobean audience would have seen the witches as genuinely evil and dangerous, and Macbeth's choice to seek them out in Act 4 as a turn towards damnation.

question.text: True or false: the witches directly instruct Macbeth to kill King Duncan.
question.hint: Read their greetings in Act 1 Scene 3 carefully. Do they give a command, or a prediction?
question.explanation: False. The witches only greet Macbeth with titles, including 'king hereafter'. The idea of murder comes from Macbeth himself, which is why the play supports a free-will reading.

activities.title: Appearance versus reality, and gender
activities.content:
## Appearance versus reality

The witches announce the theme in the first scene: *"Fair is foul, and foul is fair"*. Nothing can be trusted by its surface.

- Duncan says of the traitor Cawdor, *"There's no art / To find the mind's construction in the face"* (1.4), then immediately trusts Macbeth, the next traitor.
- Lady Macbeth tells Macbeth to *"look like the innocent flower, / But be the serpent under 't"* (1.5).
- Macbeth's *"False face must hide what the false heart doth know"* (1.7) ends the act with deception chosen.
- The apparitions' prophecies sound like guarantees but are traps.

## Gender and masculinity

Characters repeatedly link manhood to violence. Lady Macbeth asks spirits to *"unsex me here"* (1.5) because she believes womanhood is a weakness, then taunts Macbeth that he will be *"so much more the man"* if he kills. Macbeth later uses the same trick on the murderers.

Shakespeare challenges this idea through **Macduff**. When told he must take the news of his family's death *"like a man"*, he replies that he must also *"feel it as a man"* (4.3). Real manhood includes grief and love, not only violence. The play suggests that the Macbeths' narrow idea of strength is exactly what destroys them.

question.text: Complete the quotations that introduce the theme of appearance versus reality.

metadata.blanksText: The witches chant "Fair is ___, and foul is fair." Lady Macbeth tells her husband to "look like the innocent ___, / But be the serpent under 't." Macbeth ends Act 1 with "False ___ must hide what the false heart doth know."

question.hint: Opposites, a flower, and a part of the body that shows expressions.
question.explanation: 'Fair is foul' establishes reversal; the 'innocent flower' hides the serpent; the 'false face' hides the false heart.

question.text: Macduff's line "I must also feel it as a man" (4.3) challenges ideas in the play about which themes? Select **all** that apply.
question.hint: Whose idea of manhood does Macduff contradict, and what does his grief show he values over ambition?
question.explanation: Macduff's grief redefines masculinity to include feeling, contradicting Lady Macbeth's view that a man proves himself through violence. It also presents loyalty and love of family as the values a good man holds, which contrasts with Macbeth's ambition. It is not about the supernatural or fate.

options.text: Loyalty and the value of family over ambition

options.feedback: Macduff's grief has nothing to do with the witches or prophecy.

question.text:
Starting with this moment from Act 1 Scene 7, explore how Shakespeare presents ambition as a destructive force in *Macbeth*.

*Macbeth is alone. He says he has "no spur / To prick the sides of my intent, but only / Vaulting ambition, which o'erleaps itself / And falls on the other."*

Write two or three developed paragraphs. Refer to this moment **and** to the play as a whole, analyse Shakespeare's methods, and link your ideas to the play's context.
question.hint: Plan: (1) what the extract shows about ambition and how the horse-riding metaphor works, (2) one later moment where ambition leads to more violence, (3) the ending, where ambition has left Macbeth empty, (4) what a Jacobean audience would think about ambition against a rightful king.
question.explanation: A strong answer argues that ambition is presented as self-destroying. In the extract the 'vaulting' metaphor pictures ambition as a rider who leaps so hard he falls, so Macbeth predicts his own downfall; the soliloquy form lets the audience hear his conscience losing. Across the play, ambition grows into paranoia (the murder of Banquo, 'in blood stepp'd in so far') and finally emptiness ('signifying nothing'). Lady Macbeth's collapse shows the same cost. Context: Jacobean belief in the Divine Right of Kings meant ambition that reached for the crown was a sin against God's order, and the play warns James I's audience against it.

markScheme.criterion: AO1: Makes a clear argument that ambition is destructive or self-defeating in the play
AO2: Analyses the 'vaulting ambition' metaphor (rider, leaping, falling over)
AO2: Comments on the soliloquy form or the effect of hearing Macbeth's private thoughts
AO1: Refers to a later moment where ambition leads to further violence (Banquo, the Macduffs, 'in blood stepp'd')
AO1: Refers to the ending or to the emptiness ambition brings ('signifying nothing', 'brief candle', despair)
AO2: Analyses a second language method (light and dark imagery, contrast, blood imagery, verb choice)
AO3: Links ambition to Jacobean beliefs (Divine Right, Great Chain of Being, sin, James I, Gunpowder Plot)
AO1/AO3: Considers Lady Macbeth's ambition or the wider message that ambition destroys others too

activities.title: Key points
activities.content:
- **Ambition** is the tragic flaw: it 'o'erleaps itself', bringing a crown but destroying meaning.
- **Kingship vs tyranny**: Duncan and Malcolm nurture; Macbeth rules by fear and the land sickens. Context: James I and Divine Right.
- **Guilt** grows from within: blood, sleep and hands are the key motifs; Macbeth buries guilt in violence, Lady Macbeth is destroyed by it.
- **Supernatural**: the witches tempt, they do not compel; equivocation misleads by telling the truth.
- **Appearance vs reality**: 'Fair is foul'; false faces hide false hearts.
- **Gender**: violence is wrongly equated with manhood; Macduff shows that a true man must also 'feel'.
- In essays, trace each theme **across** the play and let context grow from the language.

practiceQuestions.text: Which line, spoken by the witches in the opening scene, introduces the theme of appearance versus reality?
practiceQuestions.hint: It is a chant built on opposites.
practiceQuestions.explanation: 'Fair is foul, and foul is fair' warns that good and evil will be confused throughout the play.

options.text: "Fair is foul, and foul is fair"
"Is this a dagger which I see before me"

practiceQuestions.text: True or false: Banquo hears the same prophecy as Macbeth but does not act on it by committing a crime.
practiceQuestions.hint: Compare the two men's responses to the witches.
practiceQuestions.explanation: True. Banquo is suspicious of the witches and warns that they may betray with 'honest trifles'. His restraint supports the reading that Macbeth chooses his own path.

practiceQuestions.text: Match each motif to the theme it mainly supports.
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about what cannot be washed off, what the guilty cannot do, and what the land is compared to under a tyrant.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Blood that cannot be washed away symbolises guilt; sleep is lost by the guilty; disease imagery describes Scotland under tyranny.

metadata.blanksText: King ___ I, who wrote a book about witchcraft called Daemonologie, claimed to be descended from ___, which is why the play shows that character's line of kings.

practiceQuestions.hint: The king who came to the throne in 1603, and Macbeth's friend who is murdered in Act 3.
practiceQuestions.explanation: James I believed in witches and claimed descent from Banquo, so Shakespeare presents Banquo as honourable and shows his descendants as kings.

practiceQuestions.text: Put these moments in the order they occur, showing how guilt develops in the play.
practiceQuestions.hint: Start before the murder and end with the sleepwalking.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The dagger vision (2.1) comes before the murder; the voice about sleep follows it (2.2); Banquo's ghost appears at the banquet (3.4); Lady Macbeth sleepwalks in Act 5.
order: Macbeth sees a floating dagger leading him to Duncan's room
Macbeth hears a voice cry that he has murdered sleep
Banquo's ghost appears at the banquet
Lady Macbeth sleepwalks and tries to wash her hands

practiceQuestions.text: How does Shakespeare use Macduff to challenge the play's idea that masculinity means violence? Refer to Act 4 Scene 3 in your answer.
practiceQuestions.hint: What does Macduff say he must do with his grief, and how does this contrast with Lady Macbeth's view of what makes a man?
practiceQuestions.explanation: When Malcolm urges him to take the news 'like a man', Macduff replies that he must also 'feel it as a man'. Shakespeare shows that true manhood includes grief and love for family, contradicting Lady Macbeth's view that a man proves himself by killing. Macduff then channels his feeling into justice, defeating the tyrant.

markScheme.criterion: AO1: Refers to Macduff's response to his family's deaths ('feel it as a man')
AO2: Explains the contrast with Lady Macbeth's or Macbeth's link between manhood and violence
AO1/AO3: Explains what Shakespeare suggests about true manhood (feeling, loyalty, justice, honour)

practiceQuestions.text: Which statement best describes the play's view of the witches' influence on Macbeth?
practiceQuestions.hint: Consider that Banquo hears the same words and reacts differently.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The witches tempt Macbeth with predictions but never command him. His own ambition and choices turn prophecy into murder.

options.text: They tempt him with prophecies, but his own choices lead to the murders
They force him to kill Duncan through a magic spell
options.feedback: No spell compels him; he debates the murder freely in soliloquy.

options.text: They have no influence at all on the events of the play
They order him to kill Banquo and the Macduff family

practiceQuestions.text: Which of the following are 'king-becoming graces' that Malcolm lists in Act 4 Scene 3? Select **all** that apply.
practiceQuestions.hint: Malcolm names the qualities a good king should have, the opposite of his fake confession.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Malcolm lists justice, verity (truth), temperance, stableness, bounty, perseverance, mercy, lowliness, devotion, patience, courage and fortitude. Cruelty and cunning are the tyrant's qualities.

options.feedback: Cruelty is a mark of a tyrant like Macbeth.

practiceQuestions.text:
How does Shakespeare present guilt in *Macbeth*?

Write two developed paragraphs. Compare the way guilt affects Macbeth and Lady Macbeth, analyse the language and motifs Shakespeare uses, and link your ideas to context.
practiceQuestions.hint: Macbeth's guilt is instant (voices, ghost) but he responds with more killing. Lady Macbeth's guilt is delayed but destroys her. Use the blood, sleep and hand motifs, and consider Jacobean beliefs about sin and damnation.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Macbeth's guilt appears at once: the voice crying that he has murdered sleep and the belief that the ocean cannot wash away the blood. Yet he treats guilt as something to be buried under more violence. Lady Macbeth dismisses guilt ('a little water') but the sleepwalking scene reverses her confidence: she cannot wash the imagined blood away and her fragmented prose shows a broken mind. The blood and hand motifs link the two arcs. A Jacobean audience, believing in damnation for unrepented sin, would read both as souls in torment.

markScheme.criterion: AO1: Explains Macbeth's immediate guilt after the murder (sleep, blood, Banquo's ghost)
AO1: Explains Lady Macbeth's delayed guilt in the sleepwalking scene
AO2: Analyses the blood, hand or sleep motif as a symbol of guilt
AO2: Comments on the contrast or reversal between 'a little water' and 'all the perfumes of Arabia'
AO2: Comments on form (soliloquy, prose in the sleepwalking scene, fragmented speech)
AO3: Links guilt to Jacobean beliefs about sin, damnation, conscience or hell

practiceQuestions.text: Explain what the word 'equivocation' means and give one example of how the supernatural equivocates in *Macbeth*.
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about the prophecies in Act 4 that sound safe but are traps.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Equivocation means saying something that is technically true but designed to mislead. The apparitions say no man 'of woman born' can harm Macbeth, but Macduff was born by caesarean; Birnam Wood does 'move' when soldiers carry branches.

markScheme.criterion: Defines equivocation as misleading through double meaning or half-truth
Gives a correct example (woman born / Macduff, Birnam Wood, none of woman born)

practiceQuestions.text: In Act 3 Scene 4, Macbeth admits that he keeps a paid servant in every lord's household. Which idea about kingship does this most clearly show?
practiceQuestions.hint: A king who spies on his own nobles does not trust them. What kind of ruler is that?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Spying on the thanes shows Macbeth rules through fear and suspicion rather than trust and generosity. This marks him as a tyrant, the opposite of Duncan, who rewarded loyalty openly.

options.text: Macbeth rules through fear and suspicion rather than trust, marking him as a tyrant
Macbeth is a generous king who rewards his servants well
options.feedback: Paying spies is not generosity; it is a sign of paranoia.

options.text: All the lords have already joined Malcolm's army
options.feedback: At this point most thanes are still at Macbeth's court; the desertions come later.

options.text: Macbeth is following Duncan's example of good rule
options.feedback: Duncan trusted his thanes; spying on them is the opposite of his approach.

practiceQuestions.text: Explain **two** ways Shakespeare presents Duncan as a good and rightful king, and link one of them to the play's Jacobean context.
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about how Duncan treats loyal thanes, how others describe him or react to his death, and what James I's subjects believed about a king's relationship with God.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Duncan rewards loyalty generously, giving Macbeth the title of Cawdor and promising to 'plant' him and make him grow; he is humble and gracious to his hosts. His virtues are stressed by Macbeth himself, who says they will 'plead like angels' against the murder, and after his death nature is thrown into chaos and Macduff calls the killing sacrilege. For a Jacobean audience, the king was God's anointed deputy under the Divine Right of Kings, so Duncan's goodness makes his murder a sin against heaven, not just a crime.

markScheme.criterion: AO1: Gives one way Duncan is shown as a good king (rewarding loyalty, generosity, humility, trust, 'plant thee')
AO1: Gives a second, different way (his virtues 'plead like angels', nature in chaos after his death, the murder as sacrilege, grief for him)
AO3: Links to Jacobean context (Divine Right, James I, God's anointed, Great Chain of Being)

practiceQuestions.text: Match each moment in the play to the theme it most clearly illustrates.
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about conscience, loyalty to a rightful ruler, prophecies with a catch, and what it means to be a man.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The voice crying that Macbeth has murdered sleep shows guilt destroying his peace. Macduff going to England for Malcolm shows loyalty to the rightful king. The Birnam Wood promise is an equivocation that seems to fix Macbeth's fate. Macbeth's claim that he dares do all that may become a man is the play's debate about masculinity.

pairs.left: Macbeth hears a voice cry that he has murdered sleep (2.2)
Macduff goes to England to help Malcolm raise an army against the tyrant (4.3)
Macbeth is told he is safe until Birnam Wood comes to Dunsinane (4.1)
Macbeth says he dares do all that may become a man (1.7)

practiceQuestions.text: True or false: Lady Macbeth's sleepwalking in Act 5 Scene 1 shows that guilt eventually affects her as deeply as it affects Macbeth.
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about what she tries to wash from her hands and what she says about the smell of blood.
practiceQuestions.explanation: True. Although she told Macbeth that a little water would clear them of the deed, in Act 5 she compulsively washes her hands and says all the perfumes of Arabia will not sweeten them. Guilt destroys her mind and leads to her death.

options.feedback: Her obsessive hand-washing shows guilt has overwhelmed her.

practiceQuestions.text: Complete the quotations linked to the theme of guilt.

metadata.blanksText: After the murder, Macbeth fears that not even great Neptune's ___ could wash the blood from his hand. He also hears a voice cry that Macbeth does murder ___. In Act 5, Lady Macbeth complains that the smell of the ___ is still on her hand.

practiceQuestions.hint: Neptune is the god of the sea. Think about what Macbeth loses after killing a sleeping man, and what Lady Macbeth keeps trying to wash away.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Macbeth asks whether all great Neptune's ocean will wash the blood clean. The voice says Macbeth murders sleep. Lady Macbeth says the smell of the blood is still there.

practiceQuestions.text: Malcolm's testing of Macduff in Act 4 Scene 3, where he pretends to be greedy and lustful before revealing his true virtues, explores which themes? Select **all** that apply.
practiceQuestions.hint: Malcolm shows one face and hides another, and the scene lists the qualities a good king needs.
practiceQuestions.explanation: By pretending to be vicious, Malcolm uses deception to uncover the truth, so the scene explores appearance versus reality. His list of 'king-becoming graces' explores what makes a good ruler. The scene does not involve prophecy or dreams.

options.text: Kingship and what makes a good ruler

options.feedback: No prophecy or witch is involved in this scene.
Sleep is not part of this scene.

practiceQuestions.text:
Starting with this moment from Act 3 Scene 2, explore how Shakespeare presents appearance and reality in *Macbeth*.

*As king, Macbeth prepares for the banquet. He tells Lady Macbeth that they must flatter Banquo with their eyes and tongues, making their faces "vizards to our hearts", while he secretly plans Banquo's murder. When she asks what he intends, he tells her to remain "innocent of the knowledge" until she can applaud the deed.*

Write two or three developed paragraphs. Refer to this moment **and** to the play as a whole, analyse Shakespeare's methods, and link your ideas to the play's context.
practiceQuestions.hint: Explain the 'vizards' (masks) metaphor and the dramatic irony of flattering a man Macbeth means to kill. Then trace the theme back to the witches' opening chant and the 'innocent flower' and forward to the apparitions' half-truths. Link to the Gunpowder Plot and Jacobean fears of hidden treason.
practiceQuestions.explanation: A strong answer argues that Shakespeare presents deception as central to Macbeth's world. The 'vizards' metaphor shows faces used as masks to hide murderous hearts, and the audience knows Banquo will be attacked, creating dramatic irony as Macbeth talks of honouring him. The theme is set up by the witches' paradox that fair is foul, by Lady Macbeth's advice to look like the innocent flower, and by Duncan's admission that he cannot read a mind in a face. Later, Malcolm pretends to be vicious to test Macduff, and the apparitions' equivocal promises trick Macbeth until Birnam Wood moves, while Lady Macbeth's sleepwalking exposes the truth she tried to hide. For a Jacobean audience, fresh from the Gunpowder Plot and the trial of the equivocating Jesuit Garnet, hidden treason was a real fear, and Shakespeare suggests that deception eventually destroys the deceiver.

markScheme.criterion: AO1: Makes a clear argument that characters deceive by hiding their true natures behind false appearances
AO2: Analyses the 'vizards' metaphor of faces as masks concealing the heart
AO2: Comments on the dramatic irony of flattering Banquo while planning his murder, or the audience's knowledge
AO1: Refers to an earlier example of the theme (fair is foul, the innocent flower and serpent, Duncan's 'no art', the false face)
AO1: Refers to a later example (Malcolm testing Macduff, the equivocal apparitions, Birnam Wood, the sleepwalking scene revealing the truth)
AO2: Analyses a second language method (paradox, antithesis, imagery, rhyming couplet, clothing imagery)
AO3: Links to Jacobean context (the Gunpowder Plot, James I, fear of hidden treason)
AO1/AO3: Explains the wider message that deception is eventually exposed or destroys the deceiver
